country.comment: The study examines federalism and basic sanitation policy across Brazil and its states and municipalities.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Resumo, and Abstract; PDF p. 5, Section 3

effect_estimate.comment: No econometric or inferential statistical effect estimate is reported; the paper combines qualitative legal-institutional findings with descriptive national administrative statistics from SNIS (2017), SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, and SIOP (2020).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative/descriptive — no inferential numeric effect estimate reported. The study finds that fragmented federal sanitation mandates across multiple agencies, fiscal caps and debt limits, environmental licensing and procurement bottlenecks, audit/control penalization, and weak municipal fiscal and technical capacity perpetuate vertical inequality and low basic sanitation access, particularly in smaller municipalities (<50,000 inhabitants). Descriptive secondary figures reported: only 5 Federated Units (Distrito Federal, Minas Gerais, Paraná, Rio de Janeiro, and São Paulo) had >50% of households with treated sewage while 4 states did not reach 10% (SNIS, 2017); only 43% of 3,905 surveyed municipalities had a Municipal Basic Sanitation Plan in 2017 (>60.0% in municipalities >100,000 inhabitants; 69.0% had a municipal sanitation policy; 40.5% had a council and 31% had a fund in municipalities >500,000 inhabitants), prompting 4 federal decree postponements of plan deadlines; and about 30% of 5,570 municipalities participated in sanitation public consortia in 2017.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumo and Abstract; PDF pp. 6-9, Section 3, Gráficos 1-3 and Figura 1; PDF pp. 11-12, Section 4, Gráfico 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (design ceiling = 2). Coded as 1 because the study presents descriptive administrative statistics (state sewage coverage, municipal planning instruments by city size, number of federal sanitation agencies/programs, 4 deadline postponement decrees, and federal budget declines from 2015 to 2019) alongside doctrinal/policy synthesis linking intergovernmental fragmentation and municipal capacity gaps to persistent sanitation deficits, without primary case-level direct observation or quasi-experimental testing of the mechanism operating on household access.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumo; PDF pp. 6-10, Section 3; PDF pp. 10-13, Section 4

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines federal institutional fragmentation across ministries/agencies with spatial/population eligibility cutoffs (50,000-inhabitant split between Ministry of Cities and FUNASA), intergovernmental coordination and public consortia, municipal sanitation plan mandates and repeated deadline delays, environmental licensing and procurement hurdles, agency discretion, TCU/control agency penalization, municipal councils/social control, and lack of federal technical assistance to municipalities.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: This is a legal-institutional and doctrinal-empirical policy study analyzing Brazilian constitutional/statutory provisions, federal decrees, TCU audit reports, and descriptive federal administrative data (SNIS, SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, SIOP), without a primary epidemiological/qualitative fieldwork design or systematic review search protocol; therefore, the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework applies.

sample_size.comment: No primary or analytic study sample size is defined because the paper is a national legal-institutional policy analysis using narrative literature review, federal legislation/decrees, and descriptive secondary administrative databases (citing SNIS 2017 data covering Brazil's 27 Federated Units and 5,570 municipalities, the 2017 Ministry of Cities Panorama covering 3,905 surveyed municipalities, and 2015-2019 federal budget execution from SIOP 2020).
